           Additive manufacturing enabled
         autonomous laboratory for materials
          discovery and concurrent design
           of materials and shape

                   Peter C. Collins*   and Thomas K. Ales

                 A key opportunity of additive manufacturing (AM) is the ability to produce engineered
                        structures whose design has been determined by simultaneously considering the shape
                    and material complexity. Together, the shape and material couple to govern the attending
                         properties, whether those properties are local (i.e., spatially varying) or global (i.e., load
                       bearing capacity of a part). However, the tools lack the maturity and convergency to realize
                        the dream of the simultaneous digital control of materials and shape for an optimized structure
                         to achieve a desired performance level under dynamically varying external stimuli. The tools
                         that are necessary include: AM; generative design and equivalents; gradient materials and
                      heterogeneous materials; and agent-based artificial intelligent/machine learning protocols. In
                          addition, while each of these tools requires additional investment and sustained development
                            efforts, the metals AM community faces an additional barrier due to the fact that the current
                         selection of materials available for use in AM is limited, and new alloys may be desired. To
                           realize the discovery of new materials that may be produced using advanced manufacturing
                        to manufacture advanced parts and components whose properties and performance
                       transcend what is conceived of as “state-of-the-art,” it is necessary to transform the traditional
                        laboratory ecosystem where advances are incremental and slow. One such concept is that
                          of an autonomous laboratory for materials discovery. Within such an autonomous laboratory,
                    an objective associated with a desirable shape or materials attribute (e.g., specific strength,
                           electrical conductivity, magnetic susceptibility, …), including spatially varying complexities
                            in shape and materials, would result in an AI agent and scientist collaborating to initiate
                       (perhaps under some constraint) a series of fully integrated experiments involving materials
                       composition, part shape, processing (synthesis), materials state, the corresponding properties,
                   and the statistical nature of performance. These experiments would be tightly integrated
                          into a dynamic and well-correlated multiscale digital thread that would provide the basis
                   upon which physically relevant models would be determined and exercised, leading to rapid
                       discovery of new materials as well as potentially the acceleration of new materials insertion,
                         especially for additively manufactured components. While the details of such an autonomous
                        laboratory where such articles are conceived, manufactured and tested might change, and
                        include concepts such as physical or hybrid digital/physical test beds, the overall concepts
                      remain the same. This article presents a concept of an autonomous laboratory, provides
                    examples of building block advances in experimental and analytical techniques that could
                    be leveraged to realize such laboratories, and describes some of the challenges, limitations,
                    and opportunities of such a laboratory. The article also introduces the “Burke Test,” which
                              is somewhat analogous to the Turing Test to assess AI, and provides metrics to determine
                      whether a true autonomous laboratory has been achieved.

Motivation: Autonomous laboratories for discovery
of new materials for AM
It is possible to envision engineered products and systems
comprised of individual parts whose shape and/or local mate-
rials state are concurrently digitally optimized to respond
predictably to the local fields/stimuli of a part. As a result,
parts will appear to have been “topologically optimized” or
“generatively designed,” resulting in 3D distributions of lat-
tices, trusses, and triply periodic minimal surfaces. In metal-
based struts, the local alloy composition and/or thermal his-
tory will have been tuned to result in various properties that
are desired for given volume elements (voxels) of material
and which may differ from critical property demands of adja-
cent voxels.

    publisher = "MDPI AG"

Abstract:
The flowability of a powder is a characteristic dependent on both the particle ensemble's physical properties as well as the testing equipment and conditions. In powder bed additive manufacturing processes (SLM, EBM), flowability can be used to predict the quality of the deposited powder layer. However, how representative flowability is for the powder bed layer quality is not always clear. In this work, we compared several steel powders, as well as different testing methods. Each powder had an individual combination of composition or particle size distribution. Furthermore, the flowability testing equipment and methods were selected according to standards (Tap density, Hall flow) or referring to the published literature (angle of repose, FT4 Powder Rheometer). After measuring the flowability of different samples for each testing method, we created a database to evaluate a first correlation between the different testing methods. Finally, with a Powder Rheometer, we investigated for one sample some flow properties as function of different particle size distributions.

From text 'rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 5-6'.

Fabian O. Von Rohr. The changing landscape of materials discovery. Chimia, 78 12:855-861, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2533/chimia.2024.855, doi:10.2533/chimia.2024.855. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt presents automated grinding as one component of a broader materials-discovery workflow. Automated grinding, sieving, and pelletizing already have partially available commercial solutions, but these systems may require adaptation for the strictly controlled, inert conditions needed in autonomous materials laboratories. The article identifies robotic sample preparation as a priority, alongside automation of routine tasks such as weighing, grinding, and data analysis; however, simply increasing sample throughput is not sufficient without strategic experimental design. Materials-characterization bottlenecks include the need for rapid, precise compositional analysis using techniques such as EDX, ICPMS, XPS, and RBS, as well as integrated structural and compositional measurements. Combining EDX with diffraction in one instrument could characterize both composition and structure from a single grain. The excerpt also points to machine-learning-assisted XRD analysis as a route toward fully automated PXRD/Rietveld refinement, though existing capabilities remain limited in scope and require further development. All of these approaches must ultimately operate under inert conditions. The supplied passage contains no information about Banerjee 2025, so comparisons with that work and any specific discussion of its fully automatic grinding or Rietveld-refinement implementation cannot be established from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000063

From text 'rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 4-5'.

Fabian O. Von Rohr. The changing landscape of materials discovery. Chimia, 78 12:855-861, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2533/chimia.2024.855, doi:10.2533/chimia.2024.855. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Von Rohr 2024 identifies sample preparation and characterization—not simply sample production—as major barriers to autonomous materials-discovery laboratories. Manual grinding is a persistent problem because particle-size variation and uneven mixing create irreproducibility in diffusion-limited solid-state reactions; automation could reduce preparation time and improve consistency. The excerpt also describes robotic pellet pressing as a way to produce uniform, precise samples, alongside automated sealing, modular synthesis, and integrated preparation systems. For characterization, the proposed solution is fully automated PXRD and SXRD workflows in which robots prepare and load samples, collect data, and process results. Fully automatic analysis should include rapid phase identification, lattice-parameter determination, atomic-position refinement, and Rietveld refinement of PXRD data, including complex multiphase systems; SXRD solutions and refinements should likewise be automated. High-throughput compositional analysis, including EDX, is presented as essential, while in-situ characterization could monitor phase formation and structural changes during synthesis. Crucially, Von Rohr emphasizes that increasing sample numbers is not enough: strategic experiment selection, reproducibility, and analytical throughput matter more. If analysis remains human-operated, it can remain the principal bottleneck. Banerjee 2025 is not included in the supplied excerpt, so no supported comparison with that work can be made here; likewise, the excerpt supports automated grinding conceptually but does not provide a detailed account of a specific fully automatic grinding system.

Von Rohr 2024 argues that practical automation of routine materials-discovery steps may have more immediate impact than highly publicized revolutionary autonomous-laboratory systems. He specifically identifies fully automatic grinding of solid powders, automated grinding and mixing of elements, robotic sample preparation, and automated weighing, mixing, and loading as valuable targets. Such robotics could reduce tedious manual labor, human variability, and reproducibility problems, while enabling high-throughput workflows. The excerpt also names fully automated Rietveld refinements as an incremental improvement with potentially substantial impact. For characterization, important bottlenecks remain: automating scattering experiments, developing better analysis tools for off-stoichiometric materials, and generally overcoming limitations in materials analysis. Von Rohr emphasizes that accurate prediction, synthesis, and analysis all constrain autonomous discovery, and that skilled chemists will remain necessary to create materials or supervise their creation. The excerpt does not include Banerjee 2025, so it cannot establish what that work says or whether it adds specific characterization bottlenecks. The excerpt from von Rohr 2024 presents automatic grinding as a useful but relatively mundane improvement for autonomous materials laboratories. Robotic grinding could standardize powder particle size and homogeneity, improve reproducibility, and reduce preparation time—an important benefit for higher-throughput synthesis because solid-state reactions are often diffusion-limited and depend on grain boundaries. More broadly, robotic weighing and dispensing of reactants is proposed to reduce errors and preparation time. The main characterization bottlenecks highlighted are unreliable automated phase and structure identification, especially when disorder, impurities, incomplete reactions, and unreacted starting materials are present. The A-lab’s automated Rietveld refinements reportedly produced inaccurate fits to PXRD data, missed or misinterpreted important diffraction peaks, and contributed to incorrect structural conclusions. The excerpt also emphasizes that ordered structures were often assigned where the data better supported known disordered phases, showing that compositional disorder and cation ordering remain difficult for automated workflows. In the described McCalla workflow, precursor dispensing is automated while researchers perform other sample-handling and transfer steps. For solid-state synthesis, mixing with lithium or sodium salts is traditionally performed with a mortar and pestle, whereas the solution-based workflow uses parallel processing to improve throughput. The central characterization bottleneck is X-ray diffraction rather than dispensing or manual sample transport. A combinatorial Mo-radiation transmission diffractometer produces Rietveld-quality scans from samples as small as 2 mg in about 10 minutes. Amy Lunt. A robotic workflow to screen crystal forms using powder x-ray diffraction. Text, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.17638/03178518, doi:10.17638/03178518. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not discuss von Rohr 2024 or Banerjee 2025 specifically, nor does it mention Rietveld refinements. It does, however, describe the general automation problems that those topics may address. Powder X-ray diffraction requires a chain of operations—recovering a sample, grinding it into a powder, mounting it, and collecting diffraction data—and each stage creates technical challenges for autonomous systems. In particular, solid powders are difficult to handle because they often flow poorly and experience interparticle forces such as static; the excerpt identifies grinding, mixing, and recovery as unresolved challenges in commercial automation. Lunt reports a fully automated workflow combining a dual-armed collaborative robot, a mobile robot, a liquid dispenser, and a laboratory diffractometer. The workflow developed a new method for powder sample preparation and presentation, and PXRD patterns for small-organic-compound polymorphs were comparable to manually collected data. This suggests that robotic sample preparation can produce characterization data suitable for future automated matching against crystal-structure predictions. More broadly, the excerpt frames materials characterization as a bottleneck because no commercial system then integrated crystal growth, powder processing, sample mounting, and diffraction measurement in a closed loop. It supports the relevance of fully automatic grinding and high-throughput PXRD, but provides no specific evidence about throughput rates, automated Rietveld analysis, or the claims of the two named publications.

## pqac-00000069

From text 'lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 62-69'.

Amy Lunt. A robotic workflow to screen crystal forms using powder x-ray diffraction. Text, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.17638/03178518, doi:10.17638/03178518. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides background relevant to robotic powder-XRD preparation and the characterization bottlenecks that autonomous laboratories must address, but it does not discuss von Rohr 2024, Banerjee 2025, fully automatic grinding results, Rietveld refinements, or a general survey of high-throughput characterization. It states that the automated grinding station was intended to reproduce manual mortar-and-pestle grinding and produce a homogeneous powder. Grinding is experimentally sensitive: under-grinding can preserve preferred orientation and crystallite-size inhomogeneity, whereas excessive mechanical force can induce phase changes or amorphization. These issues represent a materials-characterization bottleneck because sample preparation can alter the phase being measured. The workflow also tested direct crystallization in polypropylene, polystyrene, and glass well plates to eliminate grinding and powder transfer. This approach failed because plastic-plate amorphous backgrounds obscured crystalline peaks, glass was too thick for useful X-ray transmission, and the small well volume limited sample quantity. Background subtraction was considered inadequate for reliable peak positions and intensities. The resulting design used larger, chemically compatible 20 mL glass vials for crystallization, followed by automated solid transfer into a plate. The excerpt therefore illustrates that robotic PXRD requires not only automated grinding and handling, but also sufficient sample volume, chemically compatible vessels, low-background measurement geometry, and reliable peak-quality data for downstream analysis.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive summary table of all workflow steps in a powder-metallurgy / AM alloy development loop, organized by the seven question categories. For each step, include columns: Step, Published Automation (system name, reference, year), Measured Results (throughput, accuracy, success rate, cycle time), Gaps/Limitations, and Feasibility for 1.5 kg payload arm. Steps should cover: (1) Post-atomization powder workup: collection, sieving, splitting, mass balance, jarring/labelling, O/N/H sealing; (2) Powder characterization: SEM stub prep (EMSBot), automated SEM-EDS (AutoEMX), laser diffraction sample intro, flowability, apparent/tap density; (3) Solid specimens: part removal from build plate, sectioning, mounting, grinding/polishing (RASI), automated hardness, Archimedes density, tensile loading; (4) Charge preparation: robotic weighing (AlloyBot, Jiang biomimetic, A-Lab Quantos), crucible loading; (5) Safety; (6) Time breakdowns; (7) Arm feasibility assessment."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Step | Published automation (system, reference, year) | Measured results | Gaps / limitations | Feasibility for 1.5 kg, low-force parallel-gripper arm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Post-atomization — collect powder from atomizer** | No peer-reviewed arm-based implementation located for rePOWDER or comparable small metal-atomizer collection. Published work discusses powder recycling and sieving, not autonomous collection. | **No published throughput, success, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Powder adhesion, inaccessible collector geometry, spills, airborne combustible dust, and alloy-to-alloy cleaning remain unquantified. | **Conditional.** The arm can move a sealed collector under 1.5 kg; open pouring should instead occur in a purpose-built grounded, contained transfer station. Do not place the arm in the atomizer chamber. |
| **1. Post-atomization — load/unload sieve stack; classify six fractions** | Commercial sieve shakers automate vibration, but no peer-reviewed robotic loading/unloading workflow with alloy-development metrics was located. Von Rohr notes that automated grinding and sieving have partially available commercial solutions requiring adaptation (pqac-00000062). | **No published robotic success rate, recovery, cycle time, or cross-alloy carryover result found.** | A six-sieve stack plus 250–300 g powder may exceed payload; lids and pans can jam; retained powder adheres to mesh; cleaning and carryover dominate validation. | **Partial.** Arm can handle individual lightweight sieves, lids, and jars with fixtures; use a powered lift/clamp and stationary shaker for an assembled stack. |
| **1. Post-atomization — riffle/split powder** | No peer-reviewed robotic riffler or rotary splitter integrated into an AM-alloy loop was located. | **No published splitting precision, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Representative sampling requires controlled feed rate and validated increment geometry; cleaning inaccessible chutes between alloys is difficult. | **Reachable with dedicated equipment.** Arm can load a sealed rotary splitter or actuate indexed containers; freehand pouring is unlikely to be sufficiently repeatable. |
| **1. Post-atomization — mass balance of fractions** | Analytical balances and robot transport are mature; A-Lab and AlloyBot demonstrate robot-to-balance workflows, although not atomized-powder mass balance (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot weighing is typically under 0.5 h per multielement charge; steady-state synthesis is about one alloy h⁻¹ (pqac-00000012). **No powder-recovery validation reported.** | Static charge, powder on vessel exteriors, drafts, balance settling, and tare/container identity must be controlled. | **High.** Use capped standardized cups, balance-door automation, AprilTag/2D-code identity, and repeated gross/tare measurements. |
| **1. Post-atomization — jar, cap, label, and inventory fractions** | No peer-reviewed implementation located for robotic jarring and labelling of combustible AM metal powders. General autonomous labs demonstrate vial/rack transport (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). | **No published success, throughput, recovery, or cross-contamination metrics found.** | Screw-cap torque, liner seating, label adhesion, powder on threads, and identity reconciliation require validation. | **High for sealed jars.** Use keyed nests, low-torque caps or preassembled septum lids, barcode printing, and machine-readable verification; avoid manipulating loose powder directly. |
| **1. Post-atomization — prepare and seal O/N/H aliquots** | No peer-reviewed robotic workflow located for weighing and hermetically sealing metal-powder aliquots for inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analysis. | **No published cycle time, seal-failure rate, blank, or cross-contamination result found.** | Tiny aliquots, static, capsule folding/crimping, contamination blanks, and chain of custody are unresolved. | **Dispensing is conditional; sealing generally needs dedicated tooling.** Use a grounded enclosed dispenser plus pneumatic/electric crimper; the arm can transport capsules and sealed vials. |
| **2. Characterization — disperse powder onto SEM stub** | **EMSBot**, Milsted et al. 2025: modified 3D printer, vacuum pickup, carbon-tape stubs, and electrostatic deposition (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). | Demonstrated at 10 kV, 10 mA, 5 s exposure; pickup is retried three times before requesting a human. Dispersion was more uniform and less agglomerated than manual preparation, but no aggregate throughput or success percentage was reported (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). | High voltage and airborne-particle containment require redesign for combustible aluminium; deposition is particle-size selective and chemistry dependent. | **High for stub logistics; do not copy open electrostatic deposition for Al without a formal ignition-risk review.** A grounded, enclosed mechanical/vacuum dispersion module is preferable. |
| **2. Characterization — automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis** | DeCost et al. 2016 established autonomous computer-vision characterization; Bakas et al. 2022 reported Mask R-CNN powder segmentation. **AutoEMX/AutoEMXSp**, Giunto et al. 2025–2026, automates particle localization, EDS spots, spectral filtering, and phase clustering (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000050). | AutoEMX typically acquires about 100 spectra in 20–45 min per sample, processes tens of samples per day, and achieved compositions generally within 5–10% relative deviation across 74 samples and 38 elements (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000053). | Requires instrument API access and good dispersion; particles below roughly 2 µm are disfavoured; irregular geometry and substrate contamination still cause rejected spectra. | **High for stub exchange if the SEM has an automatable load lock; analysis is software-side.** Payload is not limiting. |
| **2. Characterization — introduce sample to laser-diffraction particle sizer** | Autosamplers and wet-dispersion units exist commercially, but no peer-reviewed arm-integrated metal-alloy workflow with recovery or carryover metrics was located. | **No relevant published robotic success rate or cycle time found.** | Representative subsampling, wet versus dry dispersion, ultrasound-induced deagglomeration, solvent compatibility, and complete line cleaning can bias PSD results. | **High for sealed-vial loading.** Use the instrument’s enclosed autosampler; avoid arm-based open pouring or aerosol-generating dry feed. |
| **2. Characterization — Hall/Carney flowability** | Published studies compare standardized manual funnels and automated rheometers; they do not report autonomous sample loading and cleaning. | No robotic metric found. Test results are method- and powder-dependent; standardized funnel tests can fail to flow for cohesive powders. | Start detection, funnel blockage, complete recovery, cleaning, humidity, and operator tapping strongly affect results. | **Moderate.** Arm can place a cup and actuate a gate; funnel filling, levelling, recovery, and cleaning should be enclosed and fixture-driven. |
| **2. Characterization — apparent and tap density** | Commercial tap-density instruments automate tapping/counting, but no peer-reviewed end-to-end robotic AM-powder workflow was located. | **No published robotic cycle time, success rate, or cross-contamination result found.** | Standardized filling, avoiding pre-compaction, reading volume, cleaning cylinders, and powder recovery remain manual. | **High for instrument tending.** Use lightweight keyed cylinders, machine vision for meniscus/bed height, and sealed transfer fixtures. |
| **3. Solid specimens — remove LPBF parts from build plate** | Industrial bandsaw, wire-EDM, and robotic machining cells automate removal, but no alloy-discovery-loop paper with general success and cycle metrics was located. | **No transferable success rate or cycle-time evidence found.** | Cutting loads, heat, swarf, supports, geometry variation, plate mass, and collision risk exceed benchtop-arm capabilities. | **Industrial equipment required.** The PiPER may tend small loose coupons after separation, not perform sawing, EDM, or high-force support removal. |
| **3. Solid specimens — section specimens** | Automated abrasive saws are commercially mature, but published closed-loop robotic loading metrics for AM alloy campaigns were not located. | **No relevant success-rate or cycle-time dataset found.** | Cutting force, coolant, guarding, clamping, blade wear, and geometry-specific fixturing dominate. | **Arm tending only.** A guarded automatic saw with pneumatic vise is required; robot should handle only lightweight, pre-fixtured samples. |
| **3. Solid specimens — hot/compression mounting** | Automated mounting presses exist commercially; no peer-reviewed robot-integrated AM-alloy workflow with measured reliability was located. | **No published robotic metric found.** | Typical mounting forces and temperatures are far beyond the arm; resin dosing and mould cleaning add contamination risks. | **Industrial press required.** Arm can load moulds/coupons using fixtures but cannot supply pressing force; cold-mount dispensing is more accessible. |
| **3. Solid specimens — grind, polish, clean, etch, and image** | **RASI**, BAM: UR5e, modified Qpol250 BOT, cleaning/etching station, and automated microscope; Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). | Up to 150 slices per specimen per day; largely unattended 24/7 operation; samples to about 15 × 15 × 15 mm³; z spacing to about 0.17 µm. Position variation is submicrometre laterally and below 1° rotationally (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). | Throughput decreases with extensive polishing, etching, or imaging; requires dedicated grinder/polisher, kinematic holders, fluid handling, and substantial integration. | **Transport feasible; polishing force is not.** PiPER can shuttle standardized pucks, but the grinder/polisher must clamp and apply load independently. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Vickers/microhardness** | Commercial automatic stages perform autofocus, indentation arrays, and image measurement; no peer-reviewed arm-loaded AM-alloy loop with reliability metrics was located. | **No published end-to-end loading success or cycle time found.** | Surface finish, focus, edge spacing, indentation recognition, and specimen tilt dominate error. | **High for puck loading** if the tester has an automatic stage and repeatable nest; the indenter supplies force. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Archimedes density** | No peer-reviewed robotic air/weighed-liquid density workflow for AM coupons was located; published AM studies generally report manual Archimedes measurements. | **No published robotic cycle time or success rate found.** | Trapped bubbles, wetting, suspension-wire contact, temperature, evaporation, open porosity, drying, and droplets on the balance cause failures. | **Moderate.** Feasible with a dedicated air/liquid balance, fixed basket, wetting protocol, drip tray, and automated drying—not by freehand robot motion alone. |
| **3. Solid specimens — load tensile coupons** | Universal test frames automate control and data acquisition, but no peer-reviewed flexible robot-loading system for AM ASTM E8 sub-size coupons with measured success was located. | **No published success rate or loading cycle found.** | Grip alignment, extensometer attachment, specimen identification, fractured-half retrieval, and pinch/crush hazards are unresolved. | **Conditional.** Arm can place light coupons into open self-centering grips; fixture actuation and alignment sensing must be provided by the test frame. |
| **4. Charge preparation — weigh powders/pieces** | **AlloyBot**, Selvaraj/Boonpetch 2026 preprint: robot, pellet dispensers, wire cutters, balance, and reusable copper crucibles (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). **Jiang et al. 2023**: dual-arm biomimetic spatula/balance dispensing (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042). **A-Lab** uses an automatic Quantos dispenser balance (pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot: approximately one alloy h⁻¹ in steady state, <0.5 h typical weighing, better than 1 at.% target accuracy, and measured compositions within EDX’s ±1 at.% uncertainty; no overall success percentage (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012). Jiang: 0.07% mean error, 0.56% SD for non-challenging solids at 200 mg, but 23.1% aggregate failure; 239–552 s for NaNO₂ robot dispenses (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043). | AlloyBot evidence is a **2026 preprint**; Jiang failures include blocked outlets, deliquescence, sticking, and balance-detection errors. Neither validates combustible Al-powder containment. | **Pieces/slugs: high. Powders: conditional.** A low-payload arm can move cups, pellets, wire and small master-alloy pieces; use enclosed gravimetric dispensing for loose Al powder. |
| **4. Charge preparation — kit and load crucible/atomizer cup** | AlloyBot robotically pours weighed elemental charges into copper crucibles and orders lower-melting elements beneath higher-melting elements (pqac-00000007). | Handles alloys up to 25 cm³ and over 100 g Ti-6Al-4V; load-lock permits melting to begin within 15 min and production of 24 alloys day⁻¹, with about 45 min daily crucible cleaning (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). | Not demonstrated for press-fit 6063 cups/plugs, rePOWDER loading, or aluminium-powder charges; press-fitting itself may require force tooling and dimensional verification. | **High for kitting and placement.** The arm can load 250–300 g charges and cups; use a guided arbor/pneumatic press for plugs and a separate force sensor or go/no-go gauge. |
| **5. Safety — combustible metal powder and autonomous robotics** | The SDL safety literature recommends RAMP/hierarchy-of-controls, authorization, monitoring, emergency stops, collision detection, constrained motion, human review, and near-miss reporting, but gives no metal-dust-specific NFPA/ATEX implementation (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). A-Lab limited campaigns to air-stable targets and operated in air rather than proving inert-powder handling (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). | **No published success/incident rate for robots handling open combustible Al powder found. No peer-reviewed validation against NFPA 484/660 or ATEX found.** | NFPA 660/484 and the adopted fire/electrical codes require a project-specific combustible-dust hazard analysis; relevant engineering issues include ignition-capable electrical/mechanical equipment, bonding/grounding, dust-tight containment, housekeeping, ventilation/collection, explosion protection or inerting, and safe isolation. Exact obligations depend on dust explosibility data, quantity, occupancy, and authority having jurisdiction. | **Do not expose an ordinary PiPER/Raspberry Pi system to classified open-powder space without AHJ-approved design.** Prefer sealed grounded containers and a negatively contained or inert glovebox/isolator with external actuators; locate nonrated electronics outside. |
| **5. Safety — published incidents and autonomous-lab practice** | Leong et al. call for systematic near-miss reporting and note that SDL safety evidence remains immature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033). | **No peer-reviewed incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder lab was located.** Absence of reports is not evidence of safety. | Public descriptions rarely provide hazardous-area classification, dust Kst/Pmax/MIE/MEC values, cleaning validation, or ignition-source assessments. | Implement human authorization for open-powder transitions, interlocked ventilation/inerting, O₂ and pressure monitoring, spill/fire response, and remote shutdown before autonomous operation. |
| **6. Labour/time evidence — powder and alloy-development loops** | McCalla 2023 reviewed semi-automated solid-state powder workflows; A-Lab and AlloyBot provide campaign-level throughput; Von Rohr identifies preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000063). | Traditional solid-state synthesis: about 5–10 samples per researcher over three days; conventional Rietveld-quality XRD about 1 h sample⁻¹. A-Lab: 355 experiments and 41 of 58 targets synthesized in 17 days, 71% target success (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). AlloyBot: one alloy h⁻¹ with <1 h daily maintenance target. | **No published time-and-motion or person-hour breakdown was located for atomization followed by collection, six-fraction sieving, splitting, jarring, O/N/H sampling, SEM preparation, and flow testing.** The lab’s 10–15 hands-on h run⁻¹ estimate therefore remains plausible but externally unvalidated. | First priority should be direct timing: timestamp every container transition and weigh operation for 10–20 runs, separating hands-on, unattended, cleaning, rework, and safety/PPE time. |
| **7. Overall PiPER deployment judgment** | Existing systems show that low-payload robots are effective chiefly as sample couriers between purpose-built modules: EMSBot for stubs, A-Lab for vessels, and RASI for mounted specimens (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000019). | Demonstrated modules span 5 s electrostatic deposition, 20–45 min automated SEM-EDS, up to 150 metallographic slices day⁻¹, and approximately one automatically weighed/melted alloy h⁻¹ (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000010). | Published systems rarely report recovery, cross-contamination, cleaning effectiveness, or long-run manipulation success—the metrics most important for FLAIME. | **Best near-term scope:** sealed-container logistics, weighing, identity/label verification, SEM-stub handling, instrument tending, and coupon transport. **Use dedicated industrial modules:** sieve-stack lifting, pressing, cutting, mounting, polishing force, tensile gripping, dust containment, and any operation in a classified combustible-dust zone. |


*Table: Step-by-step evidence map for automating a powder-metallurgy and AM alloy-development loop, including measured results, explicit publication gaps, and suitability for BYU’s 1.5 kg PiPER arm. Feasibility ratings distinguish lightweight robotic tending from operations requiring contained or industrial process equipment.*

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, parallel gripper, about 15 N available at the flange), SO-101 leader/follower arms for teleoperation and imitation learning, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags and 3D-printed fixtures. Our alloy program (FLAIME) is an AI-guided closed loop for aluminium alloys made by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF): CALPHAD screening and cost-aware Bayesian optimization choose compositions; charges of 250 to 300 g (machined 6063 cups with press-fit plugs, or bar slugs and master-alloy pieces) are atomized in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer; then the powder is collected, weighed in six size fractions, sieved, split, jarred and labelled, sampled and sealed for oxygen analysis, tested for flowability, and mounted on SEM pin stubs (seven or eight per run) for morphology and EDS; printed specimens (single tracks, density cubes, ASTM E8 sub-size tensile bars) go to Archimedes density, Vickers hardness, metallography and tensile testing. Our own schedule estimates 10 to 15 person-hours of hands-on work per atomizer run, mostly after the run, and none of it is timed yet. Aluminium powder is a combustible metal (NFPA 484, now NFPA 660); operators wear full-face respirators for open-powder work; and the arm will stay out of the atomizer chamber. Peer efforts we know of include CMU's Materials Innovation Cloud Lab (also a rePOWDER), Texas A&M's metals self-driving lab, robotic metallography efforts, and printer-based SEM powder preparation (Milsted et al. 2025, EMSBot).

Question. What is the state of the art (2015 to 2026) in automating the hands-on steps of powder-metallurgy and additive-manufacturing alloy-development loops, and which steps have measured results?
(1) Post-atomization powder workup: powder collection, sieving and classification (loading sieve shakers), riffling or splitting, mass balance, jarring and labelling, and sealing samples for O/N/H analysis. Which have been automated with arms or other equipment, with what throughput, success rate, recovery and cross-contamination control between alloys?
(2) Powder characterization sample preparation: dispersing powder onto SEM stubs, automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis, sample introduction for laser-diffraction particle sizing, and automated flowability, apparent and tap density measurements.
(3) Solid-specimen steps: removing parts from LPBF build plates, sectioning, mounting, grinding and polishing (robotic metallography), automated Archimedes density, automated Vickers or micro-hardness, and robotic loading of tensile specimens. Give reported success rates, cycle times and failure modes.
(4) Charge preparation: robotic weighing and kitting of alloy charges from pieces or powders, and crucible loading.
(5) Safety: what NFPA 484/660, ATEX or published guidance requires of robots and electronics that handle open or closed combustible metal powders (ignition sources, grounding, dust-tight enclosures, inerting), any incident reports, and how autonomous metal-powder labs (including A-Lab follow-ups under inert atmosphere) handle this.
(6) Published time-per-sample or person-hour breakdowns for powder-metallurgy or AM alloy development that show where human hands dominate, to check our estimate that post-run workup is the bottleneck.
(7) For each step, judge whether it is realistically within reach of a 1.5 kg payload, low-force arm with a parallel gripper and Raspberry Pi cameras, or needs industrial equipment (for example press forces above a tonne).

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints and conference abstracts. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about automating powder metallurgy and AM alloy development workflows.

{"plan_json": "{
  "objectives": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "objective": "Search for literature on automated powder handling, sieving, splitting, and post-atomization workup in alloy development labs",
      "rationale": "Directly addresses question (1) about post-atomization powder workup automation",
      "status": "pending",
      "result": null,
      "evaluation": null
    },
    {
      "id": 2,
      "objective": "Search for automated SEM stub preparation, particle size analysis, flowability, and powder characterization automation",

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers near-net shaping and lower per-part costs compared to casting. Lower costs depend partly on the recyclability of LPBF feedstock powder, which is only selectively melted and can be recollected and reused. As particles are spattered, condensed, or segregated by laser heat, it is essential that reliable sieving and mixing methods are used to maintain consistent feedstock characteristics.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The effects of printing, sieving, and mixing on aluminum alloy feedstock powder were characterized by three-dimensional (3D) x-ray microscopy, which was used to classify individual particles in repeatedly recycled powder. Contrary to previous recycling studies using 2D microscopy and sieve analysis to measure powder populations, a tomography-based approach showed a decrease in median particle diameter after each recycling step. By examining classified particles, we found that elongated and flattened particles with dimensions above the sieve size were retained in the virgin condition then gradually removed by repeated recycling. The tomography analysis is presented, alongside electron microscopy characterization of elemental segregation, to thoroughly describe the recyclability of a unique AM alloy and demonstrate the interpretability of tomography-based powder analysis in the context of powder metallurgy.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The Laser-based Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) process uses a laser beam to selectively melt powder particles deposited in a layer-wise fashion to manufacture components derived from Computer-Aided Design (CAD) information. During laser processing, material is ejected from the melt pool and is known as spatter. Spatter particles can have undesirable geometries for the L-PBF process, thereby compromising the quality of the powder for further reuse. An integral step in any powder replenishing and reuse procedure is the sieving process. The sieving process captures spatter particles within the exposed powder that have a diameter larger than a defined mesh size. This manuscript reports on Ti6Al4V (Grade 23) alloy powder that had been subjected to seven reuse iterations, focusing on the characterisation of powder particles that had been captured (i.e., removed) by the sieving processes. Characterisation included chemical composition focusing upon interstitial elements O, N and H (wt.%), particle morphology and particle size analysis. On review of the compositional analysis, the oxygen contents were 0.43 wt.% and 0.40 wt.% within the 63 µm and 50 µm sieve-captured powder, respectively. Additionally, it was found that a minimum of 79% and 63% of spatter particles were present within the captured powder removed by the 63 µm and 50 µm sieves, respectively.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A methodology for the automated analysis of metal powder scanning electron microscope (SEM) images towards material characterization is developed and presented. This software-based tool takes advantage of a combination of recent artificial intelligence advances (mask R-CNN), conventional image processing techniques, and SEM characterization domain knowledge to assess metal powder quality for additive manufacturing applications. SEM is being used for characterizing metal powder alloys, specifically by quantifying the diameter and number of spherical particles, which are key characteristics for assessing the quality of the analyzed powder. Usually, SEM images are manually analyzed using third-party analysis software, which can be time-consuming and often introduces user bias into the measurements. In addition, only a few non-statistically significant samples are taken into consideration for the material characterization. Thus, a method that can overcome the above challenges utilizing state-of-the-art instance segmentation models is introduced. The final proposed model achieved a total mask average precision (mAP50) 67.2 at an intersection over union of 0.5 and with prediction confidence threshold of 0.4. Finally, the predicted instance masks are further used to provide a statistical analysis that includes important metrics such as the particle size distinction.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This work aims to study the possibility of using an electrostatic drum-type separator to prepare a powder with a narrow size distribution curve for usage in additive manufacturing. The size distributions of the uncoated commercial aluminum powders ASP-30, ASP-22, and ASP-5 were analyzed. It was shown that the powders ASP-30 and ASP-22 have similar asymmetric distributions with a SPAN of 1.480 and 1.756, respectively. ASP-5 powder, in turn, has a narrow distribution with a SPAN of 0.869. ASP-30 powder was chosen for further experiment because, traditionally, separators are used to classify large-sized materials with particle size more than 100 μm. The optimal mode of electrostatic classification was proposed for the selected powder. Various classification methods, including centrifugal and electrostatic, were compared. The powders before and after classification were studied by XRD, SEM, TEM, and TG–DSC analyses. The obtained results showed that electrostatic classification does not lead to the formation of coatings on the processed powders. Electrostatic separation effectively narrows the particle size distribution, making it a suitable and valuable method to classify initial powders for additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Abstract Traditional metallography relies on the imaging of individual section planes. However, conclusions as to spatial shapes and microstructural arrangements can only be drawn to a limited extent. The idea to reconstruct three-dimensional microstructures from metallographic serial sections is therefore obvious and not at all new. However, the manual process of preparing a great number of individual sections and assembling them into image stacks is time-consuming and laborious and therefore constitutes an obstacle to frequent use. This is why the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing, or BAM for short (Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung), is developing a robot-assisted 3D metallography system performing the tasks of preparation and image acquisition on a metallographic section fully automatically and repeatedly. Preparation includes grinding, polishing and optional etching of the section surface. Image acquisition is performed using a light optical microscope with autofocus at several magnification levels. The obtained image stack is then pre-processed, segmented and converted to a 3D model resembling a microtomographic image, but with a higher lateral resolution at large volumes. As opposed to tomographic techniques, it is possible to perform traditional chemical etching for contrasting. The integration of a scanning electron microscope is in the planning stages. Studies conducted so far have demonstrated the possibility of visualizing hot gas corrosion layers, gray cast irons and ceramic-based microelectronic structures (vias).

Abstract:
<jats:p>Comprehensive materials characterization requires precise structural knowledge beyond traditional methods. The robot‐assisted automated serial‐sectioning and imaging (RASI) platform, developed at BAM, provides automated 3D metallographic reconstructions, enabling detailed microstructural analysis of technical materials. This article showcases RASI's capabilities through several case studies, including characterization of lamellar graphite in gray cast iron, porosity in sintered steel, melt pool morphology in additively manufactured 316L stainless steel, defects in metal‐ceramic packages, and oxidation behavior in an Fe‐12Cr‐2Co alloy. By automating sample handling, mechanical serial‐sectioning, etching, and optical imaging, RASI captures complex 3D microstructures with high precision and at high speed. This approach reveals microstructural features missed by 2D analysis, even using stereological assumptions. Specifically, statistically rare and large microstructural features, such as secondary phases or interconnected pores, become apparent, which 2D methods cannot reveal. The generated volumetric data can furthermore serve as quantitative reference datasets (i.e., the ‘ground truth’) essential for validating other 3D characterization techniques and computational models, helping to bridge the gap between predictive simulations and real‐world material behavior. RASI's modular design makes it a flexible tool that provides realistic 3D insights into materials, which can be used for advanced materials research, process optimization, and quality control.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We first present a Case Study – the manufacture of 1.4 m prototype mirror-segments for the European Extremely Large Telescope, undertaken by the National Facility for Ultra Precision Surfaces, at the OpTIC facility operated by Glyndwr University. Scale-up to serial-manufacture demands delivery of a 1.4 m off-axis aspheric hexagonal segment with surface precision < 10 nm RMS every four days, compared with a typical year or more for an one-off part. This requires a radically-new approach to large optics fabrication, which will inevitably propagate into wider industrial optics. We report on how these ambitious requirements have stimulated an investigation into the synergy between robots and computer numerically controlled (‘CNC’) polishing machines for optical fabrication. The objective was not to assess which is superior. Rather, it was to understand for the first time their complementary properties, leading us to operate them together as a unit, integrated in hardware and software. Three key areas are reported. First is the novel use of robots to automate currently-manual operations on CNC polishing machines, to improve work-throughput, mitigate risk of damage to parts, and reduce dependence on highly-skilled staff. Second is the use of robots to pre-process surfaces prior to CNC polishing, to reduce total process time. The third draws the threads together, describing our vision of the automated manufacturing cell, where the operator interacts at cell rather than machine level. This promises to deliver a step-change in end-to-end manufacturing times and costs, compared with either platform used on its own or, indeed, the state-of-the-art used elsewhere.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study addresses challenges in traditional manual grinding and polishing processes, such as labour shortages and the lack of real-time surface quality inspection, by developing a robotic grinding and polishing system with force feedback control. The system integrates a digital microscope for surface image capture and an artificial intelligence model for real-time surface roughness evaluation, forming a fully automated processing and inspection workflow. Using 304 stainless steel with curved surfaces, a multi-step grinding and polishing procedure was designed and simulated using RoboDK software to generate the robotic arm’s processing path. A force sensor and a PD controller were employed to measure and adjust the grinding forces, reducing the surface roughness from 2.95 µm to 0.57 µm, achieving a mirror-like finish. Additionally, a convolutional neural network (CNN) was developed and trained with post-polishing surface images and corresponding roughness values, spanning a range of 1.69 µm to 0.57 µm. The CNN model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.081 µm, enabling precise real-time surface quality inspection. This system demonstrates the potential of combining robotics and AI to enhance efficiency, precision, and surface quality in industrial grinding and polishing applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this paper, we propose a novel method for planning grinding trajectories on curved surfaces to improve the grinding efficiency of large aluminum alloy surfaces with welds and defect areas. Our method consists of three parts. Firstly, we introduce a deficiency positioning method based on a two-dimensional image and three-dimensional point cloud, which enables us to accurately and quickly locate the three-dimensional defective areas. Secondly, we propose a 2D weld positioning method based on the defect area and obtain the spatial position of the 3D weld by combining the relationship between 2D and 3D images. Additionally, we propose an orthogonal projection method from the point cloud to the aluminum alloy surface to calculate the weld reinforcement. Thirdly, we present a space spiral grinding trajectory planning method for complex curved surfaces based on the characteristics of the weld reinforcement, spatial position, and spatial position information of the defect area. This method shortens the grinding time of the defect area and improves efficiency. Simulation and experimental results show that our grinding trajectory planning method is more efficient than other grinding methods in removing defects from the surface of aluminum alloys. Moreover, the defect area after grinding is smoother than before.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT This article reviews advanced polishing, grinding and finishing processes for challenging manufacturing applications. The topics covered are machining of advanced alloys; machining of wafers; strengths of dies after machining; grinding and polishing for wafer level packages; hybrid finishing processes; magnetorheological finishing; cooling and lubrication; dental, implant and clinical applications; grinding of metal matrix composites; machining of other brittle materials; fixed abrasive polishing; vibratory finishing; and truing, kinematics and wear of tools. Findings include that a novel three-layered ice-bonded abrasive tool was proposed to polish Ti-6Al-4V. Wafer strengths and corresponding finishing processes are challenging issues for manufacturing of microelectronics devices. The processes could significantly enhance or reduce package strengths. Burrs were minimized to zero after grinding of honeycomb using a novel wheel with small asperities on its grinding surface. Polishing of silicon substrates using a fixed abrasive pad largely shortened the polishing time. Traditionally, grinding required flood coolant, which caused various environmental problems. Recently, more companies demand reduced coolant to respond to environmental requirements. Therefore, minimum quantity of lubrication has become a novel research trend for the benefits of the environment, health and costs. Innovative approaches led to good cooling, smooth surfaces ground with low roughness and low grinding forces. Abstract:

 In alignment with the Materials Genome Initiative and as the product of a workshop sponsored by the US National Science Foundation, we define a vision for materials laboratories of the future in alloys, amorphous materials, and composite materials; chart a roadmap for realizing this vision; identify technical bottlenecks and barriers to access; and propose pathways to equitable and democratic access to integrated toolsets in a manner that addresses urgent societal needs, accelerates technological innovation, and enhances manufacturing competitiveness. Spanning three important materials classes, this article summarizes the areas of alignment and unifying themes, distinctive needs of different materials research communities, key science drivers that cannot be accomplished within the capabilities of current materials laboratories, and open questions that need further community input. Here, we provide a broader context for the workshop, synopsize the salient findings, outline a shared vision for democratizing access and accelerating materials discovery, highlight some case studies across the three different materials classes, and identify significant issues that need further discussion.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is revolutionizing the aerospace, transportation, energy, and biomedical fields due to its capacity for rapid production of geometrically complex components. The advancement of alloys for AM is critical to further boost those applications. The first-generation alloys for AM largely rely on conventional commercial alloys that were originally developed under the assumption of near-equilibrium solidification. However, some of these materials are incompatible with the non-equilibrium metallurgical behavior of AM, which may face issues like high crack susceptibility. Thus, the second-generation alloy design for AM builds upon conventional alloy systems by inoculation treatments with alloying elements (e.g., zirconium) or ceramic reinforcements (e.g., titanium carbide) to achieve better material printability and properties. Meanwhile, the limitations of commercial materials underscore the need for developing novel alloys specifically tailored for AM. The third-generation empirical approach for material design adopts a knowledge-driven strategy by leveraging established metallurgical principles and empirical correlations to guide targeted composition optimization. Such trial-and-error strategies for discovering new materials face substantial bottlenecks like long development cycles and high costs. Hence, it has propelled research toward the fourth-generation paradigm—data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) assisted materials design for AM, which is an effective and innovative material solution guided by AM-specific metallurgical features. Advances in AI and robotics will shift the future paradigm of AM-specific alloy design toward an autonomous AI-Lab, which leverages an intelligent AM agent and automated high-throughput AM printing and testing for materials discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) promise an accelerated application of the scientific method. Through the automation of experimental workflows, along with autonomous experimental planning, SDLs hold the potential to greatly accelerate research in chemistry and materials discovery. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry. Abstract:
The field of materials science stands at a critical inflection point. While laboratory innovations continue to emerge at an unprecedented pace, the traditional timeline from discovery to market in 10–20 years has become an unacceptable bottleneck in addressing urgent technological challenges. We argue that self-driving laboratories (SDLs) represent not merely another step in automation, but a fundamental reimagining of the materials development pipeline. By integrating manufacturing constraints and scalability considerations from the earliest stages of discovery, SDLs can collapse the laboratory-to-factory timeline while improving reproducibility and success rates. This requires abandoning the traditional sequential approach of materials screening, device optimization and manufacturing scale-up; in favor of concurrent cross-scale development. Here, we critically examine current SDL implementations, challenge prevailing assumptions about automation in materials science, and propose a roadmap for truly integrated materials development platforms that could revolutionize how we translate laboratory discoveries into commercial products.
