Abstract:
<jats:p>This comprehensive review examines the evolution of autonomous materials synthesis laboratories that integrate artificial intelligence with advanced robotics to accelerate discovery. Traditional materials development pipelines typically require 10-20 years, but self-driving laboratories (SDLs) and Materials Acceleration Platforms (MAPs) aim to reduce this to 1-2 years through closed-loop systems combining physical experimentation with computational intelligence. The review analyzes critical components including robotic hardware architectures, integrated analytical instrumentation, closed-loop optimization strategies, AI-driven decision-making frameworks, and multi-agent systems for laboratory coordination. Case studies demonstrate remarkable success across various domains: nanomaterials synthesis, inorganic materials exploration, electrocatalyst discovery, and reaction mechanism elucidation. Large language models have recently enhanced these systems by improving knowledge extraction, experimental planning, and multi-agent coordination. The integration of standardized data formats, accessible materials databases, and sophisticated knowledge representation frameworks further accelerates discovery while enhancing reproducibility. However, a simple adaptation of AI methods and algorithms successfully exploited in one area to another field may face unexpected problems. Accelerating the discovery of new functional materials in chemical self-driving laboratories has an essential dependence on previous experimenters’ experience. Self-driving laboratories help automate and intellectualize processes involved in discovering nanomaterials with required parameters that are difficult to transfer to AI-driven systems straightforwardly. It is not easy to find a suitable design method for self-driving laboratory implementation. This paper analyzes the workflow of autonomous experimentation in the self-driving laboratory and distinguishes the core structure of such a laboratory, including sensing technologies. Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms possess the capability to accelerate the design of novel materials; however, their advancement in materials science is severely hindered by a fundamental deficit of experimental data, commonly referred to as data starvation. Unlike solution-based chemistry, where high-throughput (HT) technologies are a well-established standard, the automated synthesis of solid materials—particularly polymers and multicomponent composites—poses an extreme engineering challenge. Furthermore, the traditional, manual research model is inherently flawed by human bias, notably the systematic non-publication of negative results, which deprives AI models of critical boundary information regarding the design space. This paper is the first in a three-part review series defining the architecture of a fully automated, unbiased “data factory” for closed-loop discovery. This section focuses on the physical foundations of the HT workflow: experimental planning, automated synthesis, and material management. Emphasis is placed on the paradigm shift from classical, discrete Design of Experiments (DoE) to the novel concept of Continuous Gradient DoE. It reviews how robotic platforms utilizing precise gravimetric and volumetric feeders, integrated with extruders and in-line capillary rheology, enable the seamless, high-throughput manufacturing of thermoplastics and composites. Moreover, an innovative approach to sample logistics is presented, redefining classical storage patterns through the implementation of Continuous Material Management. This encompasses direct physical tagging (e.g., inkjet marking on continuous filaments or films), spool-based transport systems, and precise, real-time metadata mapping. As demonstrated, the integration of these systems yields an order-of-magnitude increase in productivity (generating tens of thousands of novel material variants annually), a radical reduction in unit costs, and the production of terabytes of standardized, machine-readable data. Establishing this reliable hardware and analytical infrastructure represents the essential first step toward unlocking the full potential of artificial intelligence in advanced materials engineering.</jats:p>

Compositional characterization is essential for understanding and optimizing material performance. For powder-based materials, ubiquitous across diverse technologies, accurately resolving the composition of individual phases at high throughput remains an unsolved challenge. This bottleneck slows material research and is particularly acute for autonomous laboratories, where large numbers of samples are synthesized and AI decision-making algorithms demand low-uncertainty data. Here, we integrate measurement automation, data filtering, and unsupervised machine learning to deliver a fully automated framework for high-throughput, phase-resolved compositional analysis of as-deposited powders using scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Our approach, implemented in the Python-based software AutoEMXSp, overcomes geometry-induced artifacts from irregular particle morphologies and enables accurate compositional quantification using only one experimental standard per element—including light elements conventionally difficult to quantify in powders. Validated across 74 powder samples with elements spanning nitrogen to bismuth, AutoEMXSp consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values and resolves minor or intermixed phases with high confidence. By delivering a robust, operator-free, high-throughput framework, this work paves the way for integration of powder compositional characterization into autonomous laboratory platforms, accelerating the pace of materials discovery and development.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    To close the gap between the rates of computational screening and experimental realization of novel materials
                    <jats:sup>1,2</jats:sup>
                    , we introduce the A-Lab, an autonomous laboratory for the solid-state synthesis of inorganic powders. This platform uses computations, historical data from the literature, machine learning (ML) and active learning to plan and interpret the outcomes of experiments performed using robotics. Over 17 days of continuous operation, the A-Lab realized 36 compounds from a set of 57 targets including a variety of oxides and phosphates that were identified using large-scale ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project and Google DeepMind. Synthesis recipes were proposed by natural-language models trained on the literature and optimized using an active-learning approach grounded in thermodynamics. Analysis of the failed syntheses provides direct and actionable suggestions to improve current techniques for materials screening and synthesis design. The high success rate demonstrates the effectiveness of artificial-intelligence-driven platforms for autonomous materials synthesis and motivates further integration of computations, historical knowledge and robotics.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The past decade has witnessed remarkable advancements in autonomous systems, such as automobiles that are evolving from traditional vehicles to ones capable of navigating complex environments without human intervention. Similarly, the rise of self-driving laboratories, which leverage robotics and artificial intelligence to accelerate discovery, is driving a paradigm shift in scientific research. As SDLs evolve to expand the scope of chemical processes that can be performed, it is essential to bring safety to the forefront of SDL research to ensure necessary safeguards against potential accidents that range from near-misses to catastrophic failures. This perspective examines the trajectory of self-driving laboratories, juxtaposing their development with those of other autonomous technologies, with a particular focus on safety. We explore current safety status and concerns, identify opportunities for innovation to shape this rapidly evolving landscape, and reflect on the actions the SDL community can take moving forward.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A number of methodologies are currently being exploited in order to dramatically increase the composition space explored in the design of new battery materials. This is proving necessary as commercial Li-ion battery materials have become increasingly high-performing and complex. For example, commercial cathode materials have quinary compositions with a sixth element in the coating, while a very large number of contenders are still being considered for solid electrolytes, with most of the periodic table being at play. Furthermore, the promise of accelerated design by computation and machine learning (ML) are encouraging, but they both ultimately require large amounts of quality experimental data either to fill in holes left by the computations or to be used to improve the ML models. All of this leads researchers to increase experimental throughputs. This perspective focuses on semiautomated experimental approaches where automation is only utilized in key steps where absolutely necessary in order to overcome bottlenecks while minimizing costs. Such workflows are more widely accessible to research groups as compared to fully automated systems, such that the current perspective may be useful to a wide community. The most essential steps in automation are related to characterization, with X-ray diffraction being a key bottleneck. By analyzing published workflows of both semi- and fully automated workflows, it is found herein that steps handled by researchers during the synthesis are not prohibitive in terms of overall throughput and may lead to greater flexibility, making more synthesis routes possible. Examples will be provided in this perspective of workflows that have been optimized for anodes, cathodes, and electrolytes in Li batteries, the vast majority of which are also suitable for battery technologies beyond Li.

Abstract:
Cerebral aneurysm clips are biomedical implants applied by neurosurgeons to re-approximate arterial vessel walls and prevent catastrophic aneurysmal hemorrhages in patients. Current methods of aneurysm clip production are labor intensive and time-consuming, leading to high costs per implant and limited variability in clip morphology. Metal additive manufacturing is investigated as an alternative to traditional manufacturing methods that may enable production of patient-specific aneurysm clips to account for variations in individual vascular anatomy and possibly reduce surgical complication risks. Relevant challenges to metal additive manufacturing are investigated for biomedical implants, including material choice, design limitations, postprocessing, printed material properties, and combined production methods. Initial experiments with additive manufacturing of 316 L stainless steel aneurysm clips are carried out on a selective laser melting (SLM) system. The dimensions of the printed clips were found to be within 0.5% of the dimensions of the designed clips. Hardness and density of the printed clips (213 ± 7 HV1 and 7.9 g/cc, respectively) were very close to reported values for 316 L stainless steel, as expected. No ferrite and minimal porosity is observed in a cross section of a printed clip, with some anisotropy in the grain orientation. A clamping force of approximately 1 N is measured with a clip separation of 1.5 mm. Metal additive manufacturing shows promise for use in the creation of custom aneurysm clips, but some of the challenges discussed will need to be addressed before clinical use is possible.

Abstract:
The morphology and size of the grains of the additively manufactured (AM) parts affect the mechanical properties and performance. The present research aimed to analyze the microstructure of AM parts, particularly the grain features, using image processing techniques. AMed aluminum components were fabricated using wire arc additive manufacturing based on cold metal transfer. The AA 5183 tensile samples fabricated using WAAM-CMT showed ductile behavior and the presence of the Lüder bands. Metallographic sections were prepared, and fine equiaxed grain was observed. An automatic image evaluation program for determining the specified grain features was developed. The grain features, including size, area, perimeter, and sphericity, were quantified, and the obtained results were verified, indicating a satisfactory agreement with those obtained from manual measurement. The output of the image processing technique clearly proved that the MATLAB program, as an affordable and swift approach (~ 4.8 s), can be used successfully to determine the microstructural properties. The image processing techniques could significantly improve the reliability and analysis of the microstructure, which would lead to the possibility of characterizing the microstructure in a broader range and having more details, and saving time and cost.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum–lithium alloys offer significant potential for lightweight construction, exhibiting decreased density and improved specific stiffness as the lithium content increases. The specific stiffness of these alloys improves with lithium concentrations up to 14 at%, outperforming that of pure aluminum. However, traditional casting methods, constrained by low cooling rates, result in the precipitation of brittle AlLi phases at grain boundaries when the lithium content exceeds 9 at%, limiting further enhancements in stiffness. In this work, it presents laser‐assisted additive manufacturing of binary Al–Li alloy powder with an increased lithium content of 14 at%. Unlike standard methods, this study utilizes an ultrashort pulse laser with a pulse duration of 250 fs at a wavelength of 1030 nm for the powder bed fusion process. With an average power of 150 W and a repetition rate of 32.5 MHz, it successfully demonstrates the production of highly dense Al‐Li alloy specimens. Ex situ laser‐induced breakdown spectroscopy is conducted to verify the high lithium content of the additively manufactured samples. Mechanical properties are assessed by measuring the elastic modulus and hardness. In addition, computer tomography, electron microscopy, and X‐ray diffraction techniques are utilized for quantitative porosity analysis and to characterize microstructure and constituent phases.</jats:p>

Advanced machine learning techniques to predict part quality can improve repeatability and open additive manufacturing to various industries. This study aims to accurately predict the relative density, surface roughness and hardness of AlSi10Mg samples produced by selective laser melting regarding process parameters such as scan speed, layer thickness, laser power, and hatch distance. For this purpose, data including porosity, surface hardness, and roughness were extracted from the literature, and additional measurements were performed on additive manufactured samples in the current work. This work compares five supervised machine learning algorithms, including artificial neural networks, support vector regression, kernel ridge regression, random forest, and Lasso regression. These models are evaluated based on the coefficient of determination and the mean squared error. On the basis of the computational results, the artificial neural network outperformed in predicting relative density, surface roughness, and hardness. Feature importance analysis on the compiled dataset using ANN revealed that laser power and scan speed are the most important features affecting relative density (e.g., porosity) and hardness, while scan speed and layer thickness significantly impact the surface roughness of the parts. The study identified an optimal laser power and scan speed region that achieves a relative density >  99%, surface roughness <  10 µm, and hardness >  120 HV. The results presented in this study provide significant advantages for additive manufacturing, potentially reducing experimentation costs by identifying the process parameters that optimize the quality of the fabricated parts.

Developing new high-performance alloy compositions is expensive and time-consuming. Conventional experimental alloy testing performed manually by human researchers is a primary bottleneck. To overcome this, we are building “AlloyBot”, a self-driving laboratory that can autonomously synthesize and test alloys 100× faster. Here we present the first building block: a fully automatic weighing and arc-melting system that can synthesize 1 alloy per hour (>150 alloys per week). Various innovations facilitate this process, such as a load-lock system to rapidly exchange crucibles, and four electrodes used for arc-melting. Alloys can be synthesized as buttons or cast rods, up to 25cm 3 in volume (>100g Ti-6Al-4V), and at a unit cost broadly ranging around ~100 USD/5cm 3 , driven primarily by feedstock pricing rather than human labor. Within metallurgical constraints, any element combination and composition can be synthesized on-demand. Performance is validated through the synthesis of Ti-6Al-4V alloy, Ti 20 Zr 20 Hf 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 refractory high-entropy alloy, and Zr 55 Cu 30 Ni 5 Al 10 metallic glass.

Abstract:
Urban air mobility (UAM) is a transformative mode of air transportation system technology that is targeted to carry passengers and goods in and around urban areas using electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. UAM operations are intended to be conducted in low altitudes where microscale turbulent wind flow conditions are prevalent. This introduces flight testing, certification, and operational complexities. To tackle these issues, the UAM industry, aviation authorities, and research communities across the world have provided prescriptive ways, such as the implementation of dynamic weather corridors for safe operation, classification of atmospheric disturbance levels for certification, etc., within the proposed concepts of operation (ConOps), certification standards, and guidelines. However, a notable hindrance to the efficacy of these solutions lies in the scarcity of operational UAM and observational wind data in urban environments. One way to address this deficiency in data is via microscale wind modelling, which has been long established in the context of studying atmospheric dynamics, weather forecasting, turbine blade load estimation, etc. Thus, this paper aims to provide a critical literature review of a variety of wind flow estimation and forecasting techniques that can be and have been utilized by the UAM community. Furthermore, a compare-and-contrast study of the commonly used wind flow models employed within the wind engineering and atmospheric science domain is furnished along with an overview of the urban wind flow conditions.

AlloyBot is an integrated, automated system for on-demand synthesis of bulk alloys. It combines a six-axis robotic arm mounted on a horizontal seventh axis, an automatic weighing module, and an automatic arc-melting module, coordinated by an industrial supervisory computer (AlloyBotMaster) and a data/metadata computer (AlloyBotBrain). The system can prepare alloy volumes up to 25 cm3, equivalent to more than 100 g of Ti-6Al-4V, and is currently configured for arbitrary compositions using 12 stocked metallic elements, with expansion to 24 dispenser pairs planned. The weighing module uses separate pellet and wire dispensers for each element: pellets provide coarse, economical dosing, while accurately cut wire segments provide fine mass adjustment through closed-loop balance feedback. The robot places cups on the scale, pours weighed components into a reusable copper crucible, and orders low-melting elements below higher-melting elements for charging. A weighing cycle takes less than one hour. Stated dispensing accuracy is better than 1 at.%; for a 2 mm by 1 mm wire segment, the nominal contribution is approximately 0.16 at.% in a 1 cm3 alloy and below 0.01 at.% in a 25 cm3 alloy. The excerpt describes automated repeated melting, flipping, and remelting, with optional suction casting, but gives no overall throughput beyond the sub-one-hour weighing-cycle time and no success-rate statistic.

The excerpt identifies several safety concerns for self-driving laboratories (SDLs) handling hazardous or reactive materials. Precise motion control is important because small timing or positioning errors during reagent or vessel transfer can increase risk. The authors recommend multimodal sensing for early detection of violent bubbling, excessive heat generation, and rapid pressure buildup, allowing the system to adjust reaction parameters or alert personnel. For high-stakes chemistry, a human-in-the-loop model is recommended, with stringent safety flags, frequent expert feedback, and teleoperation that keeps people away from hazardous environments. Risks become greater when SDLs optimize scaled-up reactions, even at gram scale. The proposed safety ecosystem includes open reporting of near misses, regular safety audits and peer review, training events, standardized benchmarks addressing human-robot collaboration and chemical-risk awareness, and hardware designed for chemical resistance and safe operation around humans. The excerpt also notes broader accountability and oversight concerns as human supervision decreases. However, these pages do not provide specific protocols for inert atmospheres, powder or dust control, explosion prevention, combustible-material handling, or explicit NFPA or ATEX compliance requirements. Those topics would require consultation of other sections or external standards.

Abstract:
The flowability of a powder is a characteristic dependent on both the particle ensemble's physical properties as well as the testing equipment and conditions. In powder bed additive manufacturing processes (SLM, EBM), flowability can be used to predict the quality of the deposited powder layer. However, how representative flowability is for the powder bed layer quality is not always clear. In this work, we compared several steel powders, as well as different testing methods. Each powder had an individual combination of composition or particle size distribution. Furthermore, the flowability testing equipment and methods were selected according to standards (Tap density, Hall flow) or referring to the published literature (angle of repose, FT4 Powder Rheometer). After measuring the flowability of different samples for each testing method, we created a database to evaluate a first correlation between the different testing methods. Finally, with a Powder Rheometer, we investigated for one sample some flow properties as function of different particle size distributions.

Fabian O. Von Rohr. The changing landscape of materials discovery. Chimia, 78 12:855-861, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2533/chimia.2024.855, doi:10.2533/chimia.2024.855. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt presents automated grinding as one component of a broader materials-discovery workflow. Automated grinding, sieving, and pelletizing already have partially available commercial solutions, but these systems may require adaptation for the strictly controlled, inert conditions needed in autonomous materials laboratories. The article identifies robotic sample preparation as a priority, alongside automation of routine tasks such as weighing, grinding, and data analysis; however, simply increasing sample throughput is not sufficient without strategic experimental design. Materials-characterization bottlenecks include the need for rapid, precise compositional analysis using techniques such as EDX, ICPMS, XPS, and RBS, as well as integrated structural and compositional measurements. Combining EDX with diffraction in one instrument could characterize both composition and structure from a single grain. The excerpt also points to machine-learning-assisted XRD analysis as a route toward fully automated PXRD/Rietveld refinement, though existing capabilities remain limited in scope and require further development. All of these approaches must ultimately operate under inert conditions. The supplied passage contains no information about Banerjee 2025, so comparisons with that work and any specific discussion of its fully automatic grinding or Rietveld-refinement implementation cannot be established from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000063

From text 'rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 4-5'.

Fabian O. Von Rohr. The changing landscape of materials discovery. Chimia, 78 12:855-861, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.2533/chimia.2024.855, doi:10.2533/chimia.2024.855. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Von Rohr 2024 identifies sample preparation and characterization—not simply sample production—as major barriers to autonomous materials-discovery laboratories. Manual grinding is a persistent problem because particle-size variation and uneven mixing create irreproducibility in diffusion-limited solid-state reactions; automation could reduce preparation time and improve consistency. The excerpt also describes robotic pellet pressing as a way to produce uniform, precise samples, alongside automated sealing, modular synthesis, and integrated preparation systems. For characterization, the proposed solution is fully automated PXRD and SXRD workflows in which robots prepare and load samples, collect data, and process results. Fully automatic analysis should include rapid phase identification, lattice-parameter determination, atomic-position refinement, and Rietveld refinement of PXRD data, including complex multiphase systems; SXRD solutions and refinements should likewise be automated. High-throughput compositional analysis, including EDX, is presented as essential, while in-situ characterization could monitor phase formation and structural changes during synthesis. Crucially, Von Rohr emphasizes that increasing sample numbers is not enough: strategic experiment selection, reproducibility, and analytical throughput matter more. If analysis remains human-operated, it can remain the principal bottleneck. Banerjee 2025 is not included in the supplied excerpt, so no supported comparison with that work can be made here; likewise, the excerpt supports automated grinding conceptually but does not provide a detailed account of a specific fully automatic grinding system.

Von Rohr 2024 argues that practical automation of routine materials-discovery steps may have more immediate impact than highly publicized revolutionary autonomous-laboratory systems. He specifically identifies fully automatic grinding of solid powders, automated grinding and mixing of elements, robotic sample preparation, and automated weighing, mixing, and loading as valuable targets. Such robotics could reduce tedious manual labor, human variability, and reproducibility problems, while enabling high-throughput workflows. The excerpt also names fully automated Rietveld refinements as an incremental improvement with potentially substantial impact. For characterization, important bottlenecks remain: automating scattering experiments, developing better analysis tools for off-stoichiometric materials, and generally overcoming limitations in materials analysis. Von Rohr emphasizes that accurate prediction, synthesis, and analysis all constrain autonomous discovery, and that skilled chemists will remain necessary to create materials or supervise their creation. The excerpt from von Rohr 2024 presents automatic grinding as a useful but relatively mundane improvement for autonomous materials laboratories. Robotic grinding could standardize powder particle size and homogeneity, improve reproducibility, and reduce preparation time—an important benefit for higher-throughput synthesis because solid-state reactions are often diffusion-limited and depend on grain boundaries. More broadly, robotic weighing and dispensing of reactants is proposed to reduce errors and preparation time. The main characterization bottlenecks highlighted are unreliable automated phase and structure identification, especially when disorder, impurities, incomplete reactions, and unreacted starting materials are present. The A-lab’s automated Rietveld refinements reportedly produced inaccurate fits to PXRD data, missed or misinterpreted important diffraction peaks, and contributed to incorrect structural conclusions. The excerpt also emphasizes that ordered structures were often assigned where the data better supported known disordered phases, showing that compositional disorder and cation ordering remain difficult for automated workflows. In the described McCalla workflow, precursor dispensing is automated while researchers perform other sample-handling and transfer steps. For solid-state synthesis, mixing with lithium or sodium salts is traditionally performed with a mortar and pestle, whereas the solution-based workflow uses parallel processing to improve throughput. The central characterization bottleneck is X-ray diffraction rather than dispensing or manual sample transport. A combinatorial Mo-radiation transmission diffractometer produces Rietveld-quality scans from samples as small as 2 mg in about 10 minutes. The laboratory processes 128 samples per day, corresponding to up to 46,592 XRD patterns annually. The text emphasizes that high-throughput autonomous or semiautomated laboratories must parallelize synthesis steps and automate XRD through an autosampler, programmable XYZ stage, or robotic loading and operation. Long sintering times and XRD measurement remain limiting steps; the excerpt does not establish whether fully automatic grinding or Rietveld refinement itself is automated.

The excerpt does not discuss von Rohr 2024 or Banerjee 2025 specifically, nor does it mention Rietveld refinements. It does, however, describe the general automation problems that those topics may address. Powder X-ray diffraction requires a chain of operations—recovering a sample, grinding it into a powder, mounting it, and collecting diffraction data—and each stage creates technical challenges for autonomous systems. In particular, solid powders are difficult to handle because they often flow poorly and experience interparticle forces such as static; the excerpt identifies grinding, mixing, and recovery as unresolved challenges in commercial automation. Lunt reports a fully automated workflow combining a dual-armed collaborative robot, a mobile robot, a liquid dispenser, and a laboratory diffractometer. The workflow developed a new method for powder sample preparation and presentation, and PXRD patterns for small-organic-compound polymorphs were comparable to manually collected data. This suggests that robotic sample preparation can produce characterization data suitable for future automated matching against crystal-structure predictions. More broadly, the excerpt frames materials characterization as a bottleneck because no commercial system then integrated crystal growth, powder processing, sample mounting, and diffraction measurement in a closed loop. It supports the relevance of fully automatic grinding and high-throughput PXRD, but provides no specific evidence about throughput rates, automated Rietveld analysis, or the claims of the two named publications.

## pqac-00000069

From text 'lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 62-69'.

Amy Lunt. A robotic workflow to screen crystal forms using powder x-ray diffraction. Text, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.17638/03178518, doi:10.17638/03178518. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides background relevant to robotic powder-XRD preparation and the characterization bottlenecks that autonomous laboratories must address, but it does not discuss von Rohr 2024, Banerjee 2025, fully automatic grinding results, Rietveld refinements, or a general survey of high-throughput characterization. It states that the automated grinding station was intended to reproduce manual mortar-and-pestle grinding and produce a homogeneous powder. Grinding is experimentally sensitive: under-grinding can preserve preferred orientation and crystallite-size inhomogeneity, whereas excessive mechanical force can induce phase changes or amorphization. These issues represent a materials-characterization bottleneck because sample preparation can alter the phase being measured. The workflow also tested direct crystallization in polypropylene, polystyrene, and glass well plates to eliminate grinding and powder transfer. This approach failed because plastic-plate amorphous backgrounds obscured crystalline peaks, glass was too thick for useful X-ray transmission, and the small well volume limited sample quantity. Background subtraction was considered inadequate for reliable peak positions and intensities. The resulting design used larger, chemically compatible 20 mL glass vials for crystallization, followed by automated solid transfer into a plate. The excerpt therefore illustrates that robotic PXRD requires not only automated grinding and handling, but also sufficient sample volume, chemically compatible vessels, low-background measurement geometry, and reliable peak-quality data for downstream analysis.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Step | Published automation (system, reference, year) | Measured results | Gaps / limitations | Feasibility for 1.5 kg, low-force parallel-gripper arm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Post-atomization — collect powder from atomizer** | No peer-reviewed arm-based implementation located for rePOWDER or comparable small metal-atomizer collection. Published work discusses powder recycling and sieving, not autonomous collection. | **No published throughput, success, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Powder adhesion, inaccessible collector geometry, spills, airborne combustible dust, and alloy-to-alloy cleaning remain unquantified. | **Conditional.** The arm can move a sealed collector under 1.5 kg; open pouring should instead occur in a purpose-built grounded, contained transfer station. Do not place the arm in the atomizer chamber. |
| **1. Post-atomization — load/unload sieve stack; classify six fractions** | Commercial sieve shakers automate vibration, but no peer-reviewed robotic loading/unloading workflow with alloy-development metrics was located. Von Rohr notes that automated grinding and sieving have partially available commercial solutions requiring adaptation (pqac-00000062). | **No published robotic success rate, recovery, cycle time, or cross-alloy carryover result found.** | A six-sieve stack plus 250–300 g powder may exceed payload; lids and pans can jam; retained powder adheres to mesh; cleaning and carryover dominate validation. | **Partial.** Arm can handle individual lightweight sieves, lids, and jars with fixtures; use a powered lift/clamp and stationary shaker for an assembled stack. |
| **1. Post-atomization — riffle/split powder** | No peer-reviewed robotic riffler or rotary splitter integrated into an AM-alloy loop was located. | **No published splitting precision, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Representative sampling requires controlled feed rate and validated increment geometry; cleaning inaccessible chutes between alloys is difficult. | **Reachable with dedicated equipment.** Arm can load a sealed rotary splitter or actuate indexed containers; freehand pouring is unlikely to be sufficiently repeatable. |
| **1. Post-atomization — mass balance of fractions** | Analytical balances and robot transport are mature; A-Lab and AlloyBot demonstrate robot-to-balance workflows, although not atomized-powder mass balance (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot weighing is typically under 0.5 h per multielement charge; steady-state synthesis is about one alloy h⁻¹ (pqac-00000012). **No powder-recovery validation reported.** | Static charge, powder on vessel exteriors, drafts, balance settling, and tare/container identity must be controlled. | **High.** Use capped standardized cups, balance-door automation, AprilTag/2D-code identity, and repeated gross/tare measurements. |
| **1. Post-atomization — jar, cap, label, and inventory fractions** | No peer-reviewed implementation located for robotic jarring and labelling of combustible AM metal powders. General autonomous labs demonstrate vial/rack transport (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). | **No published success, throughput, recovery, or cross-contamination metrics found.** | Screw-cap torque, liner seating, label adhesion, powder on threads, and identity reconciliation require validation. | **High for sealed jars.** Use keyed nests, low-torque caps or preassembled septum lids, barcode printing, and machine-readable verification; avoid manipulating loose powder directly. |
| **1. Post-atomization — prepare and seal O/N/H aliquots** | No peer-reviewed robotic workflow located for weighing and hermetically sealing metal-powder aliquots for inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analysis. | **No published cycle time, seal-failure rate, blank, or cross-contamination result found.** | Tiny aliquots, static, capsule folding/crimping, contamination blanks, and chain of custody are unresolved. | **Dispensing is conditional; sealing generally needs dedicated tooling.** Use a grounded enclosed dispenser plus pneumatic/electric crimper; the arm can transport capsules and sealed vials. |
| **2. Characterization — disperse powder onto SEM stub** | **EMSBot**, Milsted et al. 2025: modified 3D printer, vacuum pickup, carbon-tape stubs, and electrostatic deposition (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). | Demonstrated at 10 kV, 10 mA, 5 s exposure; pickup is retried three times before requesting a human. Dispersion was more uniform and less agglomerated than manual preparation, but no aggregate throughput or success percentage was reported (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). | High voltage and airborne-particle containment require redesign for combustible aluminium; deposition is particle-size selective and chemistry dependent. | **High for stub logistics; do not copy open electrostatic deposition for Al without a formal ignition-risk review.** A grounded, enclosed mechanical/vacuum dispersion module is preferable. |
| **2. Characterization — automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis** | DeCost et al. 2016 established autonomous computer-vision characterization; Bakas et al. 2022 reported Mask R-CNN powder segmentation. **AutoEMX/AutoEMXSp**, Giunto et al. 2025–2026, automates particle localization, EDS spots, spectral filtering, and phase clustering (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000050). | AutoEMX typically acquires about 100 spectra in 20–45 min per sample, processes tens of samples per day, and achieved compositions generally within 5–10% relative deviation across 74 samples and 38 elements (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000053). | Requires instrument API access and good dispersion; particles below roughly 2 µm are disfavoured; irregular geometry and substrate contamination still cause rejected spectra. | **High for stub exchange if the SEM has an automatable load lock; analysis is software-side.** Payload is not limiting. |
| **2. Characterization — introduce sample to laser-diffraction particle sizer** | Autosamplers and wet-dispersion units exist commercially, but no peer-reviewed arm-integrated metal-alloy workflow with recovery or carryover metrics was located. | **No relevant published robotic success rate or cycle time found.** | Representative subsampling, wet versus dry dispersion, ultrasound-induced deagglomeration, solvent compatibility, and complete line cleaning can bias PSD results. | **High for sealed-vial loading.** Use the instrument’s enclosed autosampler; avoid arm-based open pouring or aerosol-generating dry feed. |
| **2. Characterization — Hall/Carney flowability** | Published studies compare standardized manual funnels and automated rheometers; they do not report autonomous sample loading and cleaning. | No robotic metric found. Test results are method- and powder-dependent; standardized funnel tests can fail to flow for cohesive powders. | Start detection, funnel blockage, complete recovery, cleaning, humidity, and operator tapping strongly affect results. | **Moderate.** Arm can place a cup and actuate a gate; funnel filling, levelling, recovery, and cleaning should be enclosed and fixture-driven. |
| **2. Characterization — apparent and tap density** | Commercial tap-density instruments automate tapping/counting, but no peer-reviewed end-to-end robotic AM-powder workflow was located. | **No published robotic cycle time, success rate, or cross-contamination result found.** | Standardized filling, avoiding pre-compaction, reading volume, cleaning cylinders, and powder recovery remain manual. | **High for instrument tending.** Use lightweight keyed cylinders, machine vision for meniscus/bed height, and sealed transfer fixtures. |
| **3. Solid specimens — remove LPBF parts from build plate** | Industrial bandsaw, wire-EDM, and robotic machining cells automate removal, but no alloy-discovery-loop paper with general success and cycle metrics was located. | **No transferable success rate or cycle-time evidence found.** | Cutting loads, heat, swarf, supports, geometry variation, plate mass, and collision risk exceed benchtop-arm capabilities. | **Industrial equipment required.** The PiPER may tend small loose coupons after separation, not perform sawing, EDM, or high-force support removal. |
| **3. Solid specimens — section specimens** | Automated abrasive saws are commercially mature, but published closed-loop robotic loading metrics for AM alloy campaigns were not located. | **No relevant success-rate or cycle-time dataset found.** | Cutting force, coolant, guarding, clamping, blade wear, and geometry-specific fixturing dominate. | **Arm tending only.** A guarded automatic saw with pneumatic vise is required; robot should handle only lightweight, pre-fixtured samples. |
| **3. Solid specimens — hot/compression mounting** | Automated mounting presses exist commercially; no peer-reviewed robot-integrated AM-alloy workflow with measured reliability was located. | **No published robotic metric found.** | Typical mounting forces and temperatures are far beyond the arm; resin dosing and mould cleaning add contamination risks. | **Industrial press required.** Arm can load moulds/coupons using fixtures but cannot supply pressing force; cold-mount dispensing is more accessible. |
| **3. Solid specimens — grind, polish, clean, etch, and image** | **RASI**, BAM: UR5e, modified Qpol250 BOT, cleaning/etching station, and automated microscope; Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). | Up to 150 slices per specimen per day; largely unattended 24/7 operation; samples to about 15 × 15 × 15 mm³; z spacing to about 0.17 µm. Position variation is submicrometre laterally and below 1° rotationally (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). | Throughput decreases with extensive polishing, etching, or imaging; requires dedicated grinder/polisher, kinematic holders, fluid handling, and substantial integration. | **Transport feasible; polishing force is not.** PiPER can shuttle standardized pucks, but the grinder/polisher must clamp and apply load independently. |

Solid specimens — Vickers/microhardness** | Commercial automatic stages perform autofocus, indentation arrays, and image measurement; no peer-reviewed arm-loaded AM-alloy loop with reliability metrics was located. | **No published end-to-end loading success or cycle time found.** | Surface finish, focus, edge spacing, indentation recognition, and specimen tilt dominate error. | **High for puck loading** if the tester has an automatic stage and repeatable nest; the indenter supplies force. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Archimedes density** | No peer-reviewed robotic air/weighed-liquid density workflow for AM coupons was located; published AM studies generally report manual Archimedes measurements. | **No published robotic cycle time or success rate found.** | Trapped bubbles, wetting, suspension-wire contact, temperature, evaporation, open porosity, drying, and droplets on the balance cause failures. | **Moderate.** Feasible with a dedicated air/liquid balance, fixed basket, wetting protocol, drip tray, and automated drying—not by freehand robot motion alone. |
| **3. Solid specimens — load tensile coupons** | Universal test frames automate control and data acquisition, but no peer-reviewed flexible robot-loading system for AM ASTM E8 sub-size coupons with measured success was located. | **No published success rate or loading cycle found.** | Grip alignment, extensometer attachment, specimen identification, fractured-half retrieval, and pinch/crush hazards are unresolved. | **Conditional.** Arm can place light coupons into open self-centering grips; fixture actuation and alignment sensing must be provided by the test frame. |
| **4. Charge preparation — weigh powders/pieces** | **AlloyBot**, Selvaraj/Boonpetch 2026 preprint: robot, pellet dispensers, wire cutters, balance, and reusable copper crucibles (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). **Jiang et al. 2023**: dual-arm biomimetic spatula/balance dispensing (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042). **A-Lab** uses an automatic Quantos dispenser balance (pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot: approximately one alloy h⁻¹ in steady state, <0.5 h typical weighing, better than 1 at.% target accuracy, and measured compositions within EDX’s ±1 at.% uncertainty; no overall success percentage (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012). Jiang: 0.07% mean error, 0.56% SD for non-challenging solids at 200 mg, but 23.1% aggregate failure; 239–552 s for NaNO₂ robot dispenses (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043). | AlloyBot evidence is a **2026 preprint**; Jiang failures include blocked outlets, deliquescence, sticking, and balance-detection errors. Neither validates combustible Al-powder containment. | **Pieces/slugs: high. Powders: conditional.** A low-payload arm can move cups, pellets, wire and small master-alloy pieces; use enclosed gravimetric dispensing for loose Al powder. |
| **4. Charge preparation — kit and load crucible/atomizer cup** | AlloyBot robotically pours weighed elemental charges into copper crucibles and orders lower-melting elements beneath higher-melting elements (pqac-00000007). | Handles alloys up to 25 cm³ and over 100 g Ti-6Al-4V; load-lock permits melting to begin within 15 min and production of 24 alloys day⁻¹, with about 45 min daily crucible cleaning (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). | Not demonstrated for press-fit 6063 cups/plugs, rePOWDER loading, or aluminium-powder charges; press-fitting itself may require force tooling and dimensional verification. | **High for kitting and placement.** The arm can load 250–300 g charges and cups; use a guided arbor/pneumatic press for plugs and a separate force sensor or go/no-go gauge. |
| **5. Safety — combustible metal powder and autonomous robotics** | The SDL safety literature recommends RAMP/hierarchy-of-controls, authorization, monitoring, emergency stops, collision detection, constrained motion, human review, and near-miss reporting, but gives no metal-dust-specific NFPA/ATEX implementation (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). A-Lab limited campaigns to air-stable targets and operated in air rather than proving inert-powder handling (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). | **No published success/incident rate for robots handling open combustible Al powder found. No peer-reviewed validation against NFPA 484/660 or ATEX found.** | NFPA 660/484 and the adopted fire/electrical codes require a project-specific combustible-dust hazard analysis; relevant engineering issues include ignition-capable electrical/mechanical equipment, bonding/grounding, dust-tight containment, housekeeping, ventilation/collection, explosion protection or inerting, and safe isolation. Exact obligations depend on dust explosibility data, quantity, occupancy, and authority having jurisdiction. | **Do not expose an ordinary PiPER/Raspberry Pi system to classified open-powder space without AHJ-approved design.** Prefer sealed grounded containers and a negatively contained or inert glovebox/isolator with external actuators; locate nonrated electronics outside. |
| **5. Safety — published incidents and autonomous-lab practice** | Leong et al. call for systematic near-miss reporting and note that SDL safety evidence remains immature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033). | **No peer-reviewed incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder lab was located.** Absence of reports is not evidence of safety. | Public descriptions rarely provide hazardous-area classification, dust Kst/Pmax/MIE/MEC values, cleaning validation, or ignition-source assessments. | Implement human authorization for open-powder transitions, interlocked ventilation/inerting, O₂ and pressure monitoring, spill/fire response, and remote shutdown before autonomous operation. |

A-Lab: 355 experiments and 41 of 58 targets synthesized in 17 days, 71% target success (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). AlloyBot: one alloy h⁻¹ with <1 h daily maintenance target. | **No published time-and-motion or person-hour breakdown was located for atomization followed by collection, six-fraction sieving, splitting, jarring, O/N/H sampling, SEM preparation, and flow testing.** The lab’s 10–15 hands-on h run⁻¹ estimate therefore remains plausible but externally unvalidated. | First priority should be direct timing: timestamp every container transition and weigh operation for 10–20 runs, separating hands-on, unattended, cleaning, rework, and safety/PPE time. |

{"answer": "## State of the Art in Automating Hands-On Steps of Powder-Metallurgy and Additive-Manufacturing Alloy-Development Loops (2015–2026)

This review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature (2015–2026) on the automation of each hands-on step in powder-metallurgy and AM alloy-development workflows. For each step, we report what has been demonstrated with measured results, explicitly flag publication gaps, and assess feasibility for a 1.5 kg payload, low-force arm such as the AgileX PiPER.

The following table provides a step-by-step evidence map with citations, measured results, identified gaps, and feasibility assessment:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### (1) Post-Atomization Powder Workup

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that describes a robotic or automated system for the full post-atomization workup chain—powder collection, loading sieve stacks, six-fraction classification, riffling/splitting, mass balance, jarring, labelling, or sealing O/N/H aliquots—with measured throughput, success rate, recovery, or cross-contamination control between alloys.** This represents a significant gap in the literature. Von Rohr (2024) notes that "automated grinding, sieving, and pelletizing" have "partially available commercial solutions" but that "these systems may require adaptation for the strictly controlled, inert conditions needed in autonomous materials laboratories" (pqac-00000062). The closest relevant systems are mass-balance and container-transport operations demonstrated by the A-Lab and AlloyBot (discussed under charge preparation), which validate that robot-to-balance transfer of powders and solids is technically mature (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026).

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can serve as a lightweight courier for capped containers, individual sieve pans, and jars. However, a loaded six-sieve stack with 250–300 g powder and collection pans approaches or exceeds the 1.5 kg payload. Sieve loading/unloading, splitting, and O/N/H sample sealing (crimping) each require purpose-built fixtures or tools.

---

### (2) Powder Characterization Sample Preparation

**SEM stub preparation.** The EMSBot system (Milsted et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00116a) is the state of the art, using a modified Creality Ender3 Pro 3D printer with a vacuum-pickup robot and electrostatic deposition to disperse powder onto carbon-tape-mounted SEM stubs. It operates at "10 kV, 10 mA, and a 5-second hold time" and demonstrated "more uniform dispersion and greater particle separation" than manual preparation, with reduced agglomeration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). It retries stub pickup up to three times before requesting human intervention (pqac-00000001). No aggregate throughput or quantitative success rate was reported. The system is designed for integration with autonomous laboratory workflows via a "documented API, GUI, Python backend" (pqac-00000000). **Caution:** The electrostatic deposition method has not been validated for combustible aluminium powder, and open high-voltage dispersion near Al fines would require a formal ignition-risk assessment.

**Automated SEM-EDS analysis.** The AutoEMX framework (Giunto et al. 2025 preprint, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1; published 2026 in Nature Communications, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x) provides fully automated particle localization, EDS spot selection, spectral fitting, filtering, and unsupervised k-means clustering for phase-resolved compositional analysis. It "typically acquires about 100 spectra" per sample "in 20–45 minutes" and "processes tens of samples per day" (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000050). Validated across 74 powder samples and 38 elements (nitrogen to bismuth), it "consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values" and requires only "one experimental standard per element" (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

**Laser diffraction, flowability, and apparent/tap density.** No peer-reviewed robotic end-to-end workflow was found for any of these tests. Published powder-flowability studies compare standardized Hall/Carney funnels and rheometers but do not describe autonomous sample loading, cleaning, or recovery (pqac-00000062). These tests remain predominantly manual.

---

### (3) Solid-Specimen Steps

**Robotic metallography.** The most advanced published system is RASI (Robot-Assisted Automated Serial-Sectioning and Imaging), developed at BAM (Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung). It uses a "UR5e robotic arm with parallel grippers and a wrist camera, a modified Qpol250 BOT grinding/polishing unit, an etching station, an optical microscope, and a control workstation" (pqac-00000017). RASI achieves "up to 150 slices per specimen per day" in "largely unattended, continuous 24/7 operation," with "XY resolution approaching 225 nm" and z-spacing "as fine as approximately 170 nm" for specimen volumes up to "approximately 15 × 15 × 15 mm³" (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). The system uses spray-based on-demand etching consuming "approximately 1–4 mL of etchant per slice, compared with roughly 60–200 mL for immersion baths" (pqac-00000020). Demonstrated applications include AM 316L stainless steel melt pools, sintered steel porosity, and cast iron graphite (pqac-00000013). RASI was first commissioned in 2021 and uses a UR5e (5 kg payload, ±0.03 mm repeatability) with a Python interface (pqac-00000018). The Čermák et al. 2024 paper in *Practical Metallography* (DOI: 10.1515/pm-2024-0055, unobtainable) also addresses robotic metallographic sample preparation for precision and safety, but was not accessible for review.

**Automated hardness testing.** Commercial hardness testers with automated XY stages, autofocus, and indent recognition exist, but no peer-reviewed paper was found describing a robot-loaded hardness-testing loop for AM alloy development campaigns with measured loading success rate or cycle time.

**Archimedes density.** No peer-reviewed robotic Archimedes density workflow was located. Published AM studies universally report manual density measurements.

**Tensile specimen loading.** No peer-reviewed flexible robotic loading system for ASTM E8 sub-size tensile bars with measured success was located. Collins (2026) notes that "automated robots must be capable of handling arbitrary and widely varying complex geometries" and identifies multi-fingered, pneumatic, electro-adhesive, and soft grippers as solvable engineering problems (pqac-00000060).

**Part removal from build plates and sectioning.** These steps involve cutting forces, coolant, and fixturing well beyond a benchtop arm's capabilities. No alloy-development-loop paper with general robotic success metrics was located.

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can shuttle standardized metallographic pucks and small coupons between stations but cannot supply polishing force, cutting force, or pressing force. The grinder/polisher, saw, and mounting press must operate independently.

---

### (4) Charge Preparation

**AlloyBot** (Selvaraj, Boonpetch et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1; **preprint**) is the most directly relevant system. It combines "a six-axis robotic arm mounted on a horizontal seventh axis, an automatic weighing module, and an automatic arc-melting module" with 12 element channels (expandable to 24) using paired pellet dispensers and wire feeders for coarse and fine mass control (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). Stated performance targets are "one alloy per hour (>150 alloys per week)" with delivery "within three hours of a request" and "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Compositional accuracy is "better than 1 at.%" with demonstrated agreement for Ti-6Al-4V, a refractory HEA, and a metallic glass (pqac-00000010). The system handles volumes up to 25 cm³ (>100 g Ti-6Al-4V) at approximately $100/5 cm³ driven primarily by feedstock cost (pqac-00000009). No aggregate synthesis success rate was reported.

**Biomimetic solid dispensing** (Jiang et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00075c, peer-reviewed) used a dual-arm ABB YuMi robot with interchangeable 3D-printed spatulas, an analytical balance, and fuzzy-logic closed-loop control. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, "the dual-arm robot achieved an average dispensing error of 0.07% (standard deviation 0.56%)" versus −0.41% for Quantos (pqac-00000043). However, the aggregate failure rate across all 13 tested solids was 23.1% for the robot, 26.9% for Quantos, and 26.5% for Chemspeed (pqac-00000039). Dispensing times were substantially longer: "552, 517, 381, and 239 seconds at 1000, 500, 200, and 20 mg targets" for the robot vs. 40–285 s for Quantos (pqac-00000043).

**A-Lab** (Szymanski et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w, peer-reviewed, Nature) uses "a Mitsubishi robot arm" and "an automatic Quantos dispenser balance" for precursor powder dosing, followed by mixing "with ethanol and ten 5-mm ZrO₂ balls for 9 minutes in a dual asymmetric centrifuge" and transfer into alumina crucibles (pqac-00000026). Over "17 days of continuous operation," 41 of 58 targets were synthesized, a 71% success rate (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025).

**PiPER feasibility for charge prep:** The arm can move cups, pellets, wire segments, and small master-alloy pieces well within 1.5 kg. For loose aluminium powder, an enclosed gravimetric dispenser (not freehand pouring) is essential for both accuracy and safety.

---

### (5) Safety: Combustible Metal Powders and Autonomous Robotics

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that specifically addresses NFPA 484 (now NFPA 660), ATEX/IECEx, or other combustible-dust standards as applied to autonomous robotic systems handling open aluminium or other combustible metal powders.** This is a critical gap.

The most relevant SDL safety publication is Leong et al. (2024, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28, **preprint**), which recommends the "RAMP process—recognizing hazards, assessing risks, minimizing risks, and preparing for emergencies—and the hierarchy of controls" (pqac-00000032). It advocates "multimodal sensing for early detection of violent bubbling, excessive heat generation, and rapid pressure buildup," constrained motion planning, emergency stops, human-in-the-loop authorization, and systematic near-miss reporting (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). However, this paper does not mention NFPA, ATEX, combustible dust classification, dust-tight enclosures, bonding/grounding, inerting, or explosion protection.

The A-Lab deliberately restricted its campaigns to air-stable oxide and phosphate targets and operated in open air—not under inert atmosphere (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). AlloyBot operates under high-purity argon in its arc-melting chamber with a load-lock (pqac-00000009), but the safety rationale is metallurgical (oxidation prevention) rather than explosion prevention, and the weighing module appears to operate in air.

**What NFPA 660 (formerly 484) requires in general terms** (based on the standard itself, not from a peer-reviewed paper): a combustible-dust hazard analysis for the specific material; classification of electrical equipment in areas where ignitable concentrations may exist; bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment handling powder; dust-tight enclosures or ventilation/collection for dust-generating operations; housekeeping to prevent accumulation; and explosion protection (venting, suppression, or inerting) for enclosed volumes exceeding minimum explosive concentration. Standard consumer-grade electronics, including Raspberry Pi boards and unrated motor drives, are not rated for classified areas. **No published incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder laboratory was identified**, but absence of reports is not evidence of safety.

---

### (6) Time-Per-Sample and Person-Hour Breakdowns

**No published time-and-motion study or person-hour breakdown was found for the specific atomization-to-characterization workflow described in the FLAIME program** (ultrasonic atomization → collection → six-fraction sieving → splitting → jarring → O/N/H sampling → SEM stubs → flowability → printing → density/hardness/metallography/tensile testing). The lab's estimate of 10–15 person-hours per atomizer run therefore remains externally unvalidated.

The closest published comparisons come from adjacent workflows. McCalla (2023, DOI: 10.1021/acsengineeringau.3c00037, peer-reviewed) reports that traditional solid-state powder synthesis yields "approximately 5–10 samples per researcher over three days" and identifies "structural characterization" (XRD at ~1 hour/sample) as "the dominant throughput bottleneck" (pqac-00000035). Von Rohr (2024, DOI: 10.2533/chimia.2024.855, peer-reviewed) identifies both sample preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks and states: "if analysis remains human-operated, it can remain the principal bottleneck" (pqac-00000063). AlloyBot reduces synthesis labor to "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" for ~24 alloys/day throughput (pqac-00000036).

These comparisons support the intuition that post-run powder workup and characterization preparation—not the atomization run itself—dominate hands-on time.

---

### (7) Feasibility Assessment for the PiPER Arm (1.5 kg Payload, ~15 N, Parallel Gripper, Raspberry Pi Cameras)

The evidence from published autonomous-lab implementations consistently shows that low-payload collaborative robots are most effective as **sample couriers between purpose-built processing modules**, rather than as general-purpose manipulators replacing industrial equipment. The A-Lab uses UR5e arms (5 kg payload) exclusively for crucible and labware transport between stations (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). RASI similarly uses a UR5e to shuttle specimens between a grinder/polisher, etching station, and microscope (pqac-00000017). EMSBot uses a modified 3D printer for the same courier function (pqac-00000002).

**Steps realistically within reach of the PiPER:**
- Sealed-container logistics: moving capped jars, vials, SEM-stub trays, and metallographic pucks between stations
- Weighing operations: placing cups on balances, triggering tare/read cycles
- Identity verification: reading AprilTags, barcodes, and labels with wrist camera
- SEM stub exchange: picking/placing lightweight stubs from trays to SEM-compatible holders
- Instrument tending: loading coupons into hardness tester nests, automated saw fixtures, or other instruments with self-clamping mechanisms
- Simple coupon transport for tensile bars and density specimens

**Steps requiring industrial or dedicated equipment (beyond the PiPER):**
- Sieve-stack assembly/disassembly with loaded powder (weight, clamping force)
- Press-fitting 6063 cup plugs (>>15 N, typically tonnes)
- Part removal from LPBF build plates (cutting forces)
- Compression/hot mounting (kN forces, 150–180°C)
- Grinding and polishing (sustained contact force, abrasive environment)
- Operations in classified combustible-dust areas (the PiPER and Raspberry Pi are not rated for such environments)

---

### Summary of Publication Status

The AlloyBot preprint (Selvaraj et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1) and the Giunto et al. 2025 preprint (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1) are **preprints** that have not completed peer review; the latter was subsequently published in *Nature Communications* in 2026 (pqac-00000046). The Leong et al. safety perspective (DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28) is also a **preprint**. The Collins 2026 paper (DOI: 10.1557/s43577-026-01078-y) is a peer-reviewed perspective/roadmap paper that presents an aspirational framework rather than demonstrated hardware results (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059). All other principal sources cited (Szymanski et al. 2023 in *Nature*, Milsted et al. 2025 in *Digital Discovery*, Jiang et al. 2023 in *Digital Discovery*, Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 in *Practical Metallography* and *Advanced Engineering Materials*, McCalla 2023 in *ACS Engineering Au*, and Von Rohr 2024 in *Chimia*) are peer-reviewed."}
